surfaces.part: outer stone frame (top lintel band, light beige line)
lowest step (foreground), light edge line then vertical face with dividers

answer.evidence: The drawing is a head-on view of a descending staircase. Each step is a 1-row light edge line (rows 17 and 22) above a vertical riser face (rows 18-20 and 23-28) with vertical divider lines. Beyond them is a dark pit (rows 6-16) with more stacked risers. No step shows a horizontal tread band of 3 or more rows, and there is no ellipse. The only top-like parts are the 1-row edge lines. The silhouette is a near-uniform 30px wide rectangle with a frame, so the staircase reads as a front elevation, not a flat plate seen from above.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate reads as a small stair icon on a large, flat dark-grey backdrop, not a 4x3 ground patch with continuous texture like the grass and paving references. The stair has only about 3 steps per material (frame, dark recess, grey treads). Its dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, so the outline is a uniform black sticker line, whereas the grass reference has 0% neutral edge pixels and carries dark material tones. The backdrop is a large flat fill with no grain or per-stone shading, while the paving reference shades each stone individually. The measured 7 tones per tile equals the paving reference only because the tile is mostly flat plus outline, and the 8% near-flat coverage is likely understated against what I see. By eye the candidate is clearly thinner and flatter than either reference.

surfaces.part: descending step risers 1-3 (stacked bands at rows 9-12, 13-16, 18-21)
lowest step front face with light top edge line

answer.evidence: The staircase is drawn as a face-on elevation. Each step is a vertical riser band with vertical divider joints (x≈14 and x≈20) and a 1-row light edge line (rows 13, 17, 22). No step has a band of tread rows above its edge line, so the treads are not shown as horizontal surfaces. The dark recess in rows 6-12 reads as a wall opening, not a floor plate. The 1-row light line at row 22 over a 6-row face is only a rim, so the top surface is 1 row at most. The object is not a flat plate seen from above; it is a front view of stairs inside a frame.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stair icon sitting on a mostly uniform dark slate backdrop, not a continuous 4x3 ground patch like the grass and paving references. It has only 7 colours in total, and the measured 7 visible tones per tile only matches the paving reference. That figure comes from a handful of flat bands, not from grain. The stair steps and frame show about 3 lightness steps, against 5-6 on the references. The outline is neutral grey-black: 100% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, against 0% for the grass reference and 80% for the paving reference, and it reads as a sticker-like line around the frame and opening. The background and the stair faces have no per-stone shading, no speckle and no grain. The paving reference shades stones one by one, which the candidate does not. The 8% flat-coverage figure understates how flat the image looks to the eye. It would look thinner and flatter than the references if placed beside them.

surfaces.part: dark stairwell opening at the top
descending step bands, each a lighter edge line over a face with dividers

answer.evidence: The object fills a rectangular 30px-wide plate with a continuous outline frame from row 1 to row 29. It shows a dark pit at the top, with progressively lighter step bands below at rows 13-16, 17-20 and 22-28. The bands are separated by 1-row edge lines at rows 17 and 22. This reads as a stair viewed from above, the same way a flat mat or floor decal would. There is no separate vertical south face of 3 or more rows, and the bottom rows 28-29 are only the frame border. The width profile is a constant 30px, narrowing to 28 and 26 at the last two rows, which is just the border. The result is a flat plate with no standing volume, which suits the 'flat' kind.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small boxed stair icon on a dark grey backdrop, not a 4x3 ground patch that tiles like the grass and paving references. It has only 7 distinct colours in total. The stone frame and steps read as about 4 lightness steps, against roughly 6 on the paving. The dark edge pixels are 100% neutral (paving 80%), and by eye the frame is a uniform near-black/grey line that gives a sticker look. The step treads and the dark interior are large smooth fills with little grain, whereas the paving references have per-stone shading and highlight edges. The measured 7 visible tones only matches the paving reference. The 8% near-flat coverage (references 0%) and the lack of dot texture mean the piece is flatter than the references. A careful artist would not accept it next to the paving as equally rich.

surfaces.part: stair treads stepping down into the dark

answer.evidence: The object is a framed rectangle (beige border on the top, left and right, 30 px wide throughout) holding a staircase seen from above. Treads get darker toward the top, from the light bottom tread at rows 23-28 up to near-black at rows 6-12. Each step has a thin nosing line (rows 13, 17, 22) with a shadow row beneath (row 21), so the bands read as horizontal treads going down into darkness, not as a standing object. There is no standing south face of 3 or more rows and no eave or roof, so it reads as a flat plate with steps, which is acceptable for the flat kind.

styleAnswer.evidence: The reference paving is a full 4x3 ground patch with per-stone shading and grain. The candidate is a small stair icon centred on a plain dark grey field. That field is a large flat fill, and the stair itself has about 4 grey steps with little grain. The measured facts show 7 visible tones per tile, matching the paving, and 8% near-flat coverage. But 100% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, against 0% for the grass and 80% for the paving. So the frame outline is a neutral black/grey line with no material tint, which gives the sticker look. The stair treads and frame carry no stone-by-stone texture like the paving. The piece reads as an isolated object rather than a ground surface, and it would look flatter and thinner beside the references.
